title: Sinonis fallacia
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The Trojans, who know nothing of Greek cunning, burn to hear the captive's story, and he begins it, trembling and feigning. This is the second half of Sinon's lying tale, and every word of it is a performance. He says that the Greeks often wanted to give up the war and sail home, but storms kept stopping them, worst of all when the horse stood finished; so they sent Eurypylus to ask Apollo's oracle, which answered that the winds had been won with a maiden's blood, and that a Greek life must now pay for the return. At that the whole army went cold with fear. Ulysses dragged out the seer Calchas and made him name the victim; after ten days of silence Calchas, pushed hard by Ulysses, named Sinon, and everyone agreed, glad that the doom had landed on one man. Sinon says he escaped on the eve of the sacrifice and lay hidden in a marsh until the fleet had gone, and he begs the Trojans, by every god and by whatever faith still lives among men, to pity him. Priam, moved, has his bonds struck off and asks him the question that matters: why was the horse built, and what is it for? Sinon, with raised hands, calls on the heavens and declares that he is released from every Greek oath, and then tells them: the Greeks' hopes had always rested on Pallas, but once Diomedes and Ulysses stole her image from the Trojan citadel, her favour ebbed away, and she proved her anger by prodigies. Calchas then declared that they must flee over the sea and bring back new omens from Argos. The horse, he says, was built in expiation for the stolen image, and built enormous so that the Trojans could not take it through their gates; for if they harmed it, ruin would fall on Priam's kingdom, but if they brought it into the city, Asia would carry war to the walls of Greece.

sentences.t:
Tum vero ardemus scitari et quaerere causas,
ignari scelerum tantorum artisque Pelasgae.
sentences.l:
Then indeed we burn to inquire and to ask the causes,
ignorant of crimes so great and of Pelasgian craft.
sentences.i: Then we were all on fire to question him and learn the reasons, knowing nothing of crimes so vast or of Greek cunning.
sentences.n: Aeneas is still the narrator, so the verbs are 'we'. 'ardemus' is present (the vivid present of narrative); 'scitari et quaerere' are infinitives after 'ardemus' (burn to ...). 'Pelasgae' = 'Greek': the Pelasgians were the old inhabitants of Greece, and Virgil uses the name, like 'Danai' and 'Argivi', as a plain synonym for the Greeks. 'ignari' agrees with the unexpressed 'nos'. 'artis Pelasgae' is the key phrase of the whole episode: Greek craft, which the Trojans are about to meet at its best.

sentences.t: Prosequitur pavitans, et ficto pectore fatur:
sentences.l: He follows on, trembling, and with a feigned heart speaks:
sentences.i: Trembling, he went on, and with a heart that was all pretence he spoke:
sentences.n: 'Prosequitur' is the deponent 'prosequor', 'he goes on', here 'continues (his tale)'. 'pavitans' — a frequentative participle, 'quaking again and again' (the fear is acted). 'ficto pectore' — ablative of manner, 'with a feigned heart'; Aeneas the narrator gives the game away at once, as at 'simulant' in line 17. 'fatur' is the old defective verb 'for, fari', 'to speak'. The colon opens Sinon's speech.

sentences.t:
“Saepe fugam Danai Troia cupiere relicta
moliri, et longo fessi discedere bello;
sentences.l:
“Often the Danaans, Troy abandoned, desired flight
to contrive, and, wearied by the long war, to depart;
sentences.i: “Often the Greeks, with Troy left behind, longed to contrive their flight and be gone, worn out by the long war;
sentences.n: Sinon's speech opens here (Greenough's mark). 'cupiere' = 'cupiverunt' (the -ere ending for -erunt; you'll see this constantly). 'Troia relicta' is an ablative absolute, 'Troy having been left'. 'moliri' is a deponent infinitive, 'to set in motion, to contrive', and with 'discedere' it hangs on 'cupiere'. 'Danai' is the nominative plural; the Greeks are named for Danaus, an ancestor of the Argives. 'longo fessi… bello' — 'fessi' is the nominative plural of 'fessus', 'weary'. Sinon is telling the Trojans what they most want to hear: the Greeks were tired and wanted to go home anyway.

sentences.t: fecissentque utinam!
sentences.l: and would that they had done it!
sentences.i: and oh, if only they had!
sentences.n: 'fecissentque' = 'fecissent' + '-que'. 'utinam' with a pluperfect subjunctive expresses a wish that cannot now be fulfilled, 'would that they had!' Sinon steps outside his tale for a moment to address the Trojans directly, and the little cry also shows him as an unhappy man cheated of his rescue.

sentences.t:
Saepe illos aspera ponti
interclusit hiemps, et terruit Auster euntis.
sentences.l:
Often them the rough winter of the sea
shut off, and the South wind frightened them going.
sentences.i: Often the sea's savage winter weather barred their way, and the south wind frightened them as they set out.
sentences.n: 'hiemps' is Greenough's spelling of 'hiems', 'winter, storm weather' (a variant spelling with an extra 'p'). 'ponti' is the genitive of 'pontus', 'sea', and goes with 'hiemps': 'the sea's roughness of winter'. 'interclusit' — 'shut off, blocked the way' (perfect). 'Auster' is the south wind, bringer of storms. 'euntis' = 'euntes', accusative plural of the present participle, agreeing with 'illos' (these accusative plurals in -is are Greenough's regular spelling; you'll see them constantly).

sentences.t:
Praecipue, cum iam hic trabibus contextus acernis
staret equus, toto sonuerunt aethere nimbi.
sentences.l:
Especially, when now here, with beams woven of maple,
the horse stood, over all the sky the storm clouds sounded.
sentences.i: Most of all, when this horse already stood here, built up of maple timbers, the storm clouds roared across the whole sky.
sentences.n: 'Praecipue' is an adverb, 'above all'. 'cum… staret' — 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive, a circumstantial clause, 'when the horse was standing'. 'hic' is the adverb, 'here' (Sinon points, as if the horse stood before them). 'trabibus contextus acernis' — 'woven together with maple beams'; compare 'intexunt abiete costas' at line 16. 'toto… aethere' is ablative of place, 'through the whole sky'. 'sonuerunt' — storm clouds 'sounded' (thundered), a pointed answer from the gods to the Greeks' building of the horse.

sentences.t:
Suspensi Eurypylum scitantem oracula Phoebi
mittimus, isque adytis haec tristia dicta reportat:
sentences.l:
In suspense, Eurypylus, to inquire the oracles of Phoebus,
we send, and he from the shrine these grim sayings brings back:
sentences.i: In anxious suspense we sent Eurypylus to seek the oracles of Phoebus, and he brought these grim words back from the inner shrine:
sentences.n: 'Suspensi' — 'hanging (in doubt)', anxious. 'Eurypylum' is a Greek captain. 'scitantem' is a present participle, 'asking'; some texts read 'scitatum' (a supine, 'to inquire'), which gives the same sense. 'oracula Phoebi' — Phoebus is Apollo; his oracle is at Delphi. 'mittimus' — Sinon says 'we': in his story he is one of the Greeks who sent the envoy. 'adytis' — an ablative of separation, from the 'adyton', the innermost shrine. The colon opens the oracle's words.

sentences.t:
“Sanguine placastis ventos et virgine caesa,
cum primum Iliacas, Danai, venistis ad oras;
sentences.l:
“With blood you appeased the winds, and a maiden slain,
when first to the Ilian shores, Danaans, you came;
sentences.i: “With blood you quieted the winds, and with a maiden's death, when first you came to the shores of Ilium, men of Greece;
sentences.n: The oracle speaks (Greenough prints a second opening mark here, inside Sinon's speech). 'placastis' = 'placavistis' (syncopated perfect). 'virgine caesa' — ablative absolute, 'a maiden having been slain'. The allusion is to the sacrifice of Iphigenia, Agamemnon's daughter, to win a wind for the fleet; Virgil does not name her here, and 'cum primum… venistis ad oras' ('when you first came to the Ilian shores') does not fit the usual story, in which she was sacrificed at Aulis before the fleet sailed. Sinon's tale need not be consistent. 'Iliacas' — 'of Ilium', that is, Troy; 'Danai' is vocative.

sentences.t:
sanguine quaerendi reditus, animaque litandum
Argolica.
sentences.l:
by blood must the returns be sought, and by a life
of Argos atonement be made.
sentences.i: by blood must your homecoming be sought, and with an Argive life must the gods be won.”
sentences.n: 'quaerendi reditus' — 'reditus' is nominative plural (the metre makes its -us long), a poetic plural for 'a return', and 'quaerendi' is the gerundive agreeing with it, with 'sunt' understood: 'a way home is to be sought'. 'litandum' is an impersonal gerundive, 'one must make acceptable sacrifice' (the verb 'litare' means to sacrifice successfully, so as to win the god's favour); the sacrifice is 'anima… Argolica', 'with an Argive life'. Greenough prints no closing mark here, though the oracle's words end at this point; in the English alone it is closed, so that the marks balance. The oracle is the heart of Sinon's lie: it makes him the destined victim.

sentences.t:
Volgi quae vox ut venit ad auris,
obstipuere animi, gelidusque per ima cucurrit
ossa tremor, cui fata parent, quem poscat Apollo.
sentences.l:
Which utterance, when it came to the ears of the crowd,
stunned were their minds, and a chill through the deepest
bones ran a shudder, for whom the fates prepare it, whom Apollo claims.
sentences.i: When this utterance reached the common ear, every heart went numb, and an icy shudder ran through the very depths of our bones, wondering for whom the fates were making ready, whom Apollo claimed.
sentences.n: 'Volgi' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulgi', genitive of 'volgus', the common crowd; 'quae vox' is a connecting relative, 'and this utterance'. 'ut venit' — 'ut' means 'when'. 'auris' = 'aures', accusative plural. 'obstipuere' = 'obstipuerunt'. 'gelidus… tremor' — 'a cold shudder', subject of 'cucurrit', with 'per ima ossa' (to the lowest parts of the bones) between. 'cui fata parent, quem poscat Apollo' are two indirect questions with the subjunctive, 'for whom the fates prepare it, whom Apollo demands'; the verb of wondering is left out, understood.

sentences.t:
Hic Ithacus vatem magno Calchanta tumultu
protrahit in medios;
sentences.l:
Here the Ithacan the seer Calchas with great uproar
drags forth into the midst;
sentences.i: At this the man of Ithaca drags the seer Calchas out before them all, amid a great uproar;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the entrance of Ulysses, 'Ithacus', the man of Ithaca. Sinon makes him the villain of his tale. 'Calchanta' is the Greek accusative of 'Calchas', the Greek army's seer, who figures again from line 176. 'protrahit' — 'drags forward'. 'in medios' = 'into the middle (of the crowd)', 'medios' being the accusative plural masculine.

sentences.t:
quae sint ea numina divom,
flagitat;
sentences.l:
what these may be, those wills of the gods,
he demands;
sentences.i: he demands to know what these decrees of the gods may be;
sentences.n: 'quae sint ea numina divom' is an indirect question depending on 'flagitat' ('demands to know'), with the subjunctive 'sint'. 'divom' is the old genitive plural, for 'divorum' (you'll see this constantly: 'divom', 'superum', 'virum'). 'numina' means 'will, power' of the gods here; Ulysses wants Calchas to say who is the victim the oracle means.

sentences.t:
et mihi iam multi crudele canebant
artificis scelus, et taciti ventura videbant.
sentences.l:
and to me now many the cruel crime of the contriver
were foretelling, and silent saw what was to come.
sentences.i: And already many were foretelling to me the cruel crime of the plotter, and in silence foreseeing what was to come.
sentences.n: 'mihi' is a dative, 'to me'. 'canebant' is the imperfect of 'cano', here 'foretold, prophesied'. 'artificis' — 'the contriver', that is, Ulysses, whose craft is the leading theme of the whole episode. 'taciti' means 'silent', they foresaw it and said nothing. 'ventura' — neuter plural of the future participle of 'venio', 'things about to come'. Sinon tells it in a way that makes Ulysses a conspirator.

sentences.t:
Bis quinos silet ille dies, tectusque recusat
prodere voce sua quemquam aut opponere morti.
sentences.l:
Twice five days he is silent, and, screened, refuses
to betray by his voice any man or set him against death.
sentences.i: For ten days he keeps silent, and, closing himself in, refuses to name any man or hand him over to death.
sentences.n: 'Bis quinos… dies' — 'twice five days'; 'quinos' is a distributive numeral, which verse uses as a plain 'five'. 'tectus' — 'covered, screened' (by his silence, or by the refusal). 'recusat prodere… aut opponere' — 'refuses to betray or to expose': 'prodere voce sua' means 'to give away by his voice, to name', 'opponere morti' means 'to set (someone) in the way of death', 'morti' being a dative.

sentences.t:
Vix tandem, magnis Ithaci clamoribus actus,
composito rumpit vocem, et me destinat arae.
sentences.l:
Hardly at last, by the great shouts of the Ithacan driven,
by agreement he breaks his voice, and me he appoints to the altar.
sentences.i: At last, hardly, forced on by the loud urging of the Ithacan, he breaks his silence as arranged, and marks me for the altar.
sentences.n: 'Vix tandem' — 'at last, and with difficulty'. 'actus' — perfect passive participle of 'ago', 'driven'. 'composito' — an ablative used adverbially, 'by prearrangement, as agreed', and it is Sinon's way of insinuating that Ulysses and Calchas had settled the matter beforehand. 'rumpit vocem' — 'breaks his voice' (breaks the silence). 'destinat arae' — 'appoints for the altar', with a dative.

sentences.t:
Adsensere omnes, et, quae sibi quisque timebat,
unius in miseri exitium conversa tulere.
sentences.l:
They assented, all, and, what for himself each feared,
turned upon one wretch's ruin they endured.
sentences.i: All agreed; and the doom that each had feared for himself they accepted, now that it was turned to the destruction of one unhappy man.
sentences.n: 'Adsensere' and 'tulere' = 'adsenserunt', 'tulerunt' (the -ere ending). 'quae sibi quisque timebat' — 'what each one feared for himself', a relative clause that is the object of 'tulere'. 'conversa' agrees with 'quae': 'turned (so as to fall) on the ruin of one wretched man'. 'tulere' here is 'bore, put up with', and the point is the easy acquiescence of a crowd: the fear of each is gone once it falls on another.

sentences.t: Iamque dies infanda aderat;
sentences.l: And now the day unspeakable was at hand;
sentences.i: And now the dreadful day was at hand;
sentences.n: 'infanda' is the same word as 'infandum' at line 3: 'not to be spoken of'. 'aderat' is the imperfect, 'was there', as the story moves back to the moment before the sacrifice.

sentences.t:
mihi sacra parari,
et salsae fruges, et circum tempora vittae:
sentences.l:
for me the rites to be prepared,
and the salted grain, and around the temples the fillets:
sentences.i: the rites were being made ready for me, the salted meal, and the fillets about my brow:
sentences.n: 'sacra parari' is a historic infinitive (the infinitive used for the main verb of a narrative, a lively construction; 'mihi' is a dative of the person for whom). The victim was prepared as at a Roman sacrifice: 'salsae fruges' is the 'mola salsa', the grain mixed with salt and sprinkled over the head of the victim, and 'vittae' are the woollen fillets bound around it. The colon leads into Sinon's own action.

sentences.t:
eripui, fateor, leto me, et vincula rupi,
limosoque lacu per noctem obscurus in ulva
delitui, dum vela darent, si forte dedissent.
sentences.l:
I snatched, I confess, myself from death, and the chains I broke,
and in a muddy lake through the night, hidden in the sedge,
I lay concealed, until they should set sail, if perhaps they had.
sentences.i: I tore myself from death, I confess it, and broke my chains, and through the night I lay hidden in the reeds of a muddy pool, waiting for them to spread sail, if by chance they should.
sentences.n: 'eripui… me' — 'I snatched myself away', with 'leto' (ablative of separation, 'from death'). 'fateor' — 'I admit': Sinon makes confession a sign of honesty. 'ulva' is sedge or marsh grass. 'delitui' is the perfect of 'delitesco', 'hid myself'. 'dum vela darent' — 'dum' with the subjunctive, 'until they should set sail' (to give sail is to set it). 'si forte dedissent' is a pluperfect subjunctive in a secondary sequence, standing for a future perfect: 'if perhaps they should have set sail'. The Latin sentence trails away, as does his hope.

sentences.t:
Nec mihi iam patriam antiquam spes ulla videndi,
nec dulcis natos exoptatumque parentem;
sentences.l:
Nor for me now the ancient homeland any hope of seeing,
nor sweet sons and the longed-for father;
sentences.i: And now I have no hope of seeing my old homeland again, or my dear sons and the father I long for;
sentences.n: 'Nec mihi… spes ulla videndi' — 'spes' with a gerund, 'hope of seeing', with the dative 'mihi', 'I have'. The objects of 'videndi' are 'patriam antiquam' and, after the second 'nec', 'natos' and 'parentem'. 'exoptatum' means 'much desired', the 'ex-' being intensive. 'dulcis' is the accusative plural in -is for 'dulces'. An appeal to family feeling.

sentences.t:
quos illi fors et poenas ob nostra reposcent
effugia, et culpam hanc miserorum morte piabunt.
sentences.l:
whom they, perhaps, even, penalties for my
escape will exact, and this fault with the death of the wretched will expiate.
sentences.i: and perhaps they will demand a penalty from these dear ones for my escape, and wipe out my fault with the death of the unhappy.
sentences.n: 'quos' is a connecting relative, 'these (sons and father)'. 'fors et' is 'fors' (chance, used here as 'perhaps') with 'et' ('even'), 'perhaps indeed'. 'poenas… reposcent' — 'will exact a penalty'; 'ob nostra… effugia' — 'on account of my escapes'; the plural 'effugia' is a poetic plural for the single flight. 'culpam hanc' — the 'fault' of having escaped, which the Greeks will treat as a crime. 'piabunt' — 'will expiate'; 'miserorum' is the genitive of the wretched family, who will die in his place.

sentences.t:
Quod te per superos et conscia numina veri,
per si qua est quae restet adhuc mortalibus usquam
intemerata fides, oro, miserere laborum
tantorum, miserere animi non digna ferentis.”
sentences.l:
Wherefore you, by the gods above and the divinities conscious of truth,
by whatever, if any there is, which still remains to mortals anywhere,
untainted faith, I beg, pity the labours
so great, pity a spirit bearing what it does not deserve.”
sentences.i: So I implore you, by the gods above and the powers that know what is true, by any untarnished good faith that still survives anywhere among mortals: pity such great sufferings, pity a heart that bears what it has not deserved.”
sentences.n: 'Quod' is a connecting adverbial accusative, 'wherefore'. 'te per superos… oro' — the verb 'oro' is held back until the third line, a long suspension of the appeal. 'conscia numina veri' — 'divine powers aware of the truth'; 'veri' is a genitive after 'conscia'. 'si qua est quae restet' — 'if there is any (faith) which may still remain'; 'restet' is a subjunctive in a relative clause of characteristic. 'intemerata fides' — 'unviolated trust'. 'miserere' is the imperative of the deponent 'misereor', 'pity', which takes the genitive ('laborum', 'animi'). 'non digna ferentis' — 'ferentis' is a genitive singular present participle, 'of one who bears things not deserved'. The closing mark is Greenough's: the speech which opened at line 108 ends here. (The English closes the oracle's words at line 119, so that the marks balance.)

sentences.t: His lacrimis vitam damus, et miserescimus ultro.
sentences.l: To these tears life we give, and pity him, moreover.
sentences.i: At these tears we spare his life, and, unasked, we even pity him.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Aeneas speaks again. 'His lacrimis' is a dative ('to these tears we give life'): the tears have won it. 'ultro' means 'of one's own accord, besides', a little beyond what was needed; 'miserescimus' is an inceptive verb ('we begin to feel pity'). The Trojans' pity is exactly what Sinon's performance was meant to produce.

sentences.t:
Ipse viro primus manicas atque arta levari
vincla iubet Priamus, dictisque ita fatur amicis:
sentences.l:
Himself, to the man, first the manacles and the tight
bonds to be loosed orders Priam, and with friendly words thus speaks:
sentences.i: Priam himself is first to order the manacles and the tight bonds lifted from the man, and speaks to him in kindly words:
sentences.n: 'Ipse… primus Priamus' — the king himself leads the kindness. 'viro' is a dative of the person from whom. 'levari' is a passive infinitive after 'iubet', 'orders to be lightened (lifted)'. 'manicas atque arta… vincla' — the two nouns are accusatives, the subject of 'levari'. 'dictis… amicis' is ablative of means, 'with friendly words'.

sentences.t: “Quisquis es, amissos hinc iam obliviscere Graios;
sentences.l: “Whoever you are, the lost Greeks from here now forget;
sentences.i: “Whoever you are, from now on forget the Greeks you have lost;
sentences.n: Priam speaks (the opening mark is Greenough's). 'Quisquis es' — 'whoever you are', a polite formula, as if the man's name and standing did not matter now. 'amissos' means 'lost' (a perfect participle, 'those who have been lost to you'). 'obliviscere' is the imperative of the deponent 'obliviscor', 'forget', and takes the accusative. 'Graios' is the accusative plural of 'Graius', yet another name for the Greeks.

sentences.t: noster eris, mihique haec edissere vera roganti:
sentences.l: ours you will be, and to me these things tell true, asking:
sentences.i: you shall be one of us; and tell me truthfully what I ask:
sentences.n: 'noster eris' — 'you shall be ours' (a promise of adoption). 'edissere' is the imperative of 'edissero', 'set forth, explain'. 'mihi… roganti' — a dative of the person asking, 'to me asking', for 'what I ask'. 'haec… vera' — 'these things, true'. The colon introduces Priam's four questions.

sentences.t: Quo molem hanc immanis equi statuere?
sentences.l: For what purpose this mass of a huge horse did they set up?
sentences.i: Why did they raise this vast bulk of a horse?
sentences.n: 'Quo' is 'to what end?' (literally 'whither'). 'molem hanc immanis equi' — 'immanis' is genitive singular, agreeing with 'equi' ('of the monstrous horse'), so 'molem… equi' is the horse's bulk. 'statuere' = 'statuerunt'. The first of Priam's four questions, and the one that goes to the heart of what the horse is.

sentences.t: Quis auctor?
sentences.l: Who the author?
sentences.i: Who was behind it?
sentences.n: 'auctor' — the person who prompted or contrived it, the one responsible for the horse. 'est' is understood.

sentences.t: Quidve petunt?
sentences.l: Or what do they seek?
sentences.i: Or what do they seek by it?
sentences.n: 'Quidve' is 'quid' with '-ve' (a form of 'vel', 'or'): 'or what'. 'petunt' has the Greeks as the unexpressed subject: 'what do they aim at?'

sentences.t: Quae religio, aut quae machina belli?”
sentences.l: What sacred rite, or what engine of war?”
sentences.i: Is it an act of worship, or a war-machine?”
sentences.n: 'religio' here means 'a religious observance', and the question puts the alternative: 'religio' (an act of worship) or 'machina belli' (a siege engine). Greenough's closing mark is here: Priam's speech runs from 148 to this point.

sentences.t: Dixerat.
sentences.l: He had spoken.
sentences.i: Priam had finished.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat' is a pluperfect with the sense 'he had said (all he had to say)', a regular formula for ending a speech, after which the next speaker takes up. The sentence stands alone, a full stop between the two speeches.

sentences.t:
Ille, dolis instructus et arte Pelasga,
sustulit exutas vinclis ad sidera palmas:
sentences.l:
He, with tricks equipped and Pelasgian art,
lifted freed from bonds to the stars his palms:
sentences.i: The other, schooled in deceit and Greek cunning, raised his hands, now freed from their bonds, to the stars:
sentences.n: 'Ille' is Sinon. 'dolis instructus et arte Pelasga' — 'instructus' is the perfect participle of 'instruo', 'equipped, furnished', and the ablatives 'dolis… arte' say with what; the narrator's verdict on him, again, and 'arte Pelasga' echoes line 106. 'exutas vinclis' — 'exutas' is from 'exuo', 'strip off', 'freed from', with 'vinclis' (Greenough's 'vinclis' for 'vinculis') in the ablative. 'ad sidera' means 'to the stars', the gesture of prayer, palms held up.

sentences.t:
“Vos, aeterni ignes, et non violabile vestrum
“testor numen ait vos arae ensesque nefandi,
quos fugi, vittaeque deum, quas hostia gessi:
sentences.l:
“You, eternal fires, and your inviolable
“divinity I call to witness, he says, you altars and accursed swords,
which I fled, and fillets of the gods, which as a victim I wore:
sentences.i: “Eternal fires, and your power that no hand may violate, I call to witness, he says; you altars, and you wicked swords that I escaped, you fillets of the gods that I wore as a victim:
sentences.n: Sinon's second speech opens (it runs to 194). Greenough prints a second opening mark at the head of 155, inside the speech with no mark closing the first; it is left in the Latin and the literal English, and left out of the free English. 'aeterni ignes' are the heavenly bodies, stars and sun, as gods. 'testor' — 'I call to witness' (deponent), taking 'vos… numen' as objects; 'ait' is a parenthetic 'he says', splitting the invocation. 'vestrum' is a possessive adjective in the neuter ('vestrum numen'), 'non violabile', 'that cannot be violated'. 'ensesque nefandi' are the sacrificial knives; 'quos fugi' — 'which I fled'; 'deum' is the old genitive plural, for 'deorum'; 'quas hostia gessi' — 'hostia' is in apposition to 'ego': 'which I as a victim wore'.

sentences.i: It is lawful for me to undo the Greeks' sworn obligations, lawful to hate them, and to bring into the light whatever they hide;
sentences.n: 'fas' is divine law, what is right in the sight of the gods; with 'est' understood, 'fas mihi' is 'it is right for me', and 'resolvere', 'odisse' and 'ferre' are the infinitives. 'Graiorum' is a genitive plural. 'sacrata… iura' — 'sworn obligations'. 'sub auras' — 'out to the air', so 'into the open'. 'si qua tegunt' — 'if they conceal any (things)', 'qua' being the neuter plural after 'si'. Sinon argues that the gods themselves release him from his oath, which suits what follows, where he is going to betray the Greeks' secrets.

sentences.t: teneor patriae nec legibus ullis.
sentences.l: I am held by my homeland's laws not at all.
sentences.i: No law of my country binds me.
sentences.n: 'teneor' — 'I am held, bound'; 'patriae… legibus ullis' is an ablative of means, and with 'nec' means 'by no laws'. The sentence is a flat declaration of cutting the ties.

sentences.t:
Tu modo promissis maneas, servataque serves
Troia fidem, si vera feram, si magna rependam.
sentences.l:
You only by your promises abide, and saved, may you keep,
Troy, faith, if true things I bring, if great things I repay.
sentences.i: Only do you, Troy, stand by your promises, and, saved, keep faith with me, if what I tell is true, if I repay you richly.
sentences.n: 'Tu modo' — 'you only', addressed to Troy as a person ('Troia' is vocative or nominative). 'maneas' and 'serves' are jussive subjunctives (wishes, 'may you…'). 'servata… serves' is a play on words, 'saved, may you keep': Troy, when saved, is to keep faith. 'promissis' is an ablative: 'abide by'. 'si vera feram, si magna rependam' — 'if I bring true things, if I repay greatly', two present subjunctive conditions. The bargain is: your promise of safety against my information.

sentences.t:
Omnis spes Danaum et coepti fiducia belli
Palladis auxiliis semper stetit.
sentences.l:
All the hope of the Danaans and the confidence of the begun war
in Pallas's aid always stood.
sentences.i: All the Greeks' hope, and their trust in the war they had begun, always rested on the help of Pallas.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the heart of Sinon's lie. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural (you'll see this constantly). 'coepti… belli' — 'of the war begun'. 'Palladis auxiliis' — Pallas is Athena, whose help the Greeks had enjoyed throughout. 'stetit' — 'stood firm', 'rested'. The sentence ends mid-line, and the next begins on the same line.

sentences.t:
Impius ex quo
Tydides sed enim scelerumque inventor Ulixes,
fatale adgressi sacrato avellere templo
Palladium, caesis summae custodibus arcis,
sentences.l:
Impious, from when
the son of Tydeus, but indeed, and the contriver of crimes, Ulysses,
the fateful thing attempting from the hallowed temple to tear,
the Palladium, the guards of the high citadel slain,
sentences.i: But from the day when impious Diomede, son of Tydeus, and Ulysses, deviser of crimes, undertook to tear the fateful Palladium from its hallowed temple, killing the guards of the high citadel,
sentences.n: 'Impius ex quo' — 'ex quo' means 'from the time when', and 'impius' agrees with 'Tydides'; the full sentence runs 'ex quo… ex illo' (169). 'Tydides' is a patronymic, 'son of Tydeus', that is, Diomedes. 'sed enim' — 'but indeed', used to break in, as it were, on a thought. 'Ulixes' — compare 'Ulixi' at line 7. 'fatale… Palladium' — the Palladium was an ancient wooden image of Pallas kept in Troy's citadel, and on its presence the city's safety was believed to depend; Diomedes and Ulysses are said to have stolen it. 'adgressi' is a perfect participle of a deponent verb, 'having attempted'. 'sacrato… templo' is an ablative of separation. 'caesis… custodibus' — an ablative absolute. The sentence continues in the next unit.

sentences.t:
corripuere sacram effigiem, manibusque cruentis
virgineas ausi divae contingere vittas;
sentences.l:
they seized the sacred image, and with hands bloodied
the maiden fillets dared of the goddess to touch;
sentences.i: seized the holy image, and with bloodstained hands dared to touch the virgin goddess's fillets;
sentences.n: 'corripuere' = 'corripuerunt'. 'effigiem' — the image, the Palladium. 'manibus… cruentis' — ablative of means, their hands bloodied by the murder of the guards. 'ausi' is the perfect participle of the semi-deponent 'audeo' ('dared'; perfect 'ausus sum'), with 'contingere'. 'virgineas… vittas' — Pallas Athena is the virgin goddess, and the fillets are those on her statue.

sentences.t:
ex illo fluere ac retro sublapsa referri
spes Danaum, fractae vires, aversa deae mens.
sentences.l:
from that time to ebb, and backward slipping to be borne
the hope of the Danaans, broken the strength, turned away the goddess's mind.
sentences.i: From that day the hope of the Greeks drained away and, slipping back, was swept backward; their strength was shattered, and the goddess's mind turned from them.
sentences.n: 'ex illo' picks up 'ex quo' of line 163: 'from that time'. 'fluere' and 'referri' are historic infinitives, as in line 132, and the picture is a tide or a river flowing away. 'sublapsa' is a participle, 'slipping away', agreeing with 'spes'. 'fractae vires, aversa deae mens' — two short verbless clauses, 'est' left out; 'aversa' means 'turned away'.

sentences.t: Nec dubiis ea signa dedit Tritonia monstris.
sentences.l: Nor by doubtful portents these signs gave Tritonia.
sentences.i: Nor did Tritonian Pallas give those signs by any doubtful portents.
sentences.n: 'Tritonia' is a title of Athena (Pallas Minerva), used by Virgil as a name in its own right. 'dubiis… monstris' — 'monstris' is an ablative of means; 'dubiis' with 'nec', 'not uncertain': the portents were clear. 'signa' means 'signs' (of her anger).

sentences.t:
Vix positum castris simulacrum, arsere coruscae
luminibus flammae arrectis, salsusque per artus
sudor iit, terque ipsa solo—mirabile dictu—
emicuit, parmamque ferens hastamque trementem.
sentences.l:
Scarcely placed in the camp the image, blazed flashing
flames from eyes upturned, and salt through the limbs
sweat went, and thrice herself from the ground — wonderful to say —
sprang forth, bearing a shield and a quivering spear.
sentences.i: Hardly was the image set down in the camp when flashing flames blazed from its staring eyes, salt sweat ran over its limbs, and three times the goddess herself — a marvel to speak of — leapt up from the ground, carrying shield and quivering spear.
sentences.n: 'Vix positum… simulacrum' — 'positum' is a participle with 'est' left out, 'hardly had the image been set down', and the clause runs straight into 'arsere' with no 'cum'. 'arsere' = 'arserunt'. 'luminibus arrectis' — an ablative phrase, 'in the eyes uplifted' (staring). 'salsus sudor' — 'salt sweat', a portent. 'iit' is the perfect of 'eo', 'went', a contracted form of 'ivit'. 'ipsa' — 'she herself', the image taken as the goddess. 'mirabile dictu' — 'wonderful to say', 'dictu' being a supine. 'emicuit' — 'leapt out, flashed forth'. 'parmam' is a small shield; 'hastam trementem' — a spear shaking.

sentences.t:
Extemplo temptanda fuga canit aequora Calchas,
nec posse Argolicis exscindi Pergama telis,
omina ni repetant Argis, numenque reducant,
quod pelago et curvis secum avexere carinis.
sentences.l:
At once to be tried by flight he sings the seas, Calchas,
and that cannot by Argive weapons be destroyed Pergamum,
unless the omens they seek again at Argos, and the divinity bring back,
which over the sea and in curved ships with them they carried off.
sentences.i: At once Calchas prophesies that the seas must be tried in flight, and that Troy cannot be razed by Argive weapons unless they fetch fresh omens from Argos and bring back the divine presence that they carried off with them over the sea in their curved ships.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Calchas returns, now giving the Greeks his reading of the portents. 'Extemplo' means 'immediately'. 'canit' — 'sings' in the sense of 'prophesies'; it governs two accusative-and-infinitive constructions, 'aequora temptanda (esse)' (the gerundive of obligation) and 'nec posse Pergama exscindi'. 'Pergama' is the citadel, standing for the whole of Troy. 'ni repetant… reducant' — 'ni' ('unless') with the present subjunctive. 'omina repetant Argis' — 'seek the omens again at Argos', i.e. to take the auspices afresh at home; 'numen' is the divine presence of the Palladium, 'quod… avexere' — 'avexere' = 'avexerunt'. A lie, but a skilful one: the Greek departure is made to seem a plan.

sentences.t:
Et nunc, quod patrias vento petiere Mycenas,
arma deosque parant comites, pelagoque remenso
improvisi aderunt:
sentences.l:
And now, that to their native Mycenae by wind they have gone,
arms and gods they prepare as companions, and the sea re-measured,
unforeseen they will be here:
sentences.i: And as for their having gone off before the wind to their home in Mycenae, they are gathering arms and gods to be their companions, and when they have crossed the sea again they will be upon us unlooked-for:
sentences.n: 'quod… petiere' — 'quod' here introduces a fact, 'as to the fact that', and 'petiere' = 'petiverunt'. 'patrias… Mycenas' — Mycenae, Agamemnon's city, is in the plural, as often in Latin. 'arma deosque parant comites' — 'comites' is a predicate, 'as companions'. 'pelago remenso' — an ablative absolute with the perfect participle of 'remetior', used in a passive sense, 'the sea having been measured again'. 'improvisi' — 'unforeseen', and 'aderunt' is a future: 'they will be here'. Sinon's story explains the empty beach as a departure for fresh help, while the Greeks are in fact hidden nearby.

sentences.t: ita digerit omina Calchas.
sentences.l: thus sets in order the omens Calchas.
sentences.i: so Calchas arranges and reads the omens.
sentences.n: 'digerit omina' — 'sets out, interprets', literally 'arranges' the omens; 'ita' means 'in this manner'. 'canit' above and 'digerit' here are both present: Sinon reports Calchas's reading as if it were still going on. A short sentence to close the prophecy.

sentences.t:
Hanc pro Palladio moniti, pro numine laeso
effigiem statuere, nefas quae triste piaret.
sentences.l:
This, in place of the Palladium, warned, in place of the divinity wronged,
image they set up, which was to atone for the sad sacrilege.
sentences.i: In place of the Palladium, so warned, in requital for the wronged godhead, they have set up this image, to atone for the grim sacrilege.
sentences.n: 'Hanc… effigiem' — the horse, presented as a statue to replace the stolen image. 'moniti' is a perfect participle, 'warned' (by Calchas), agreeing with the unexpressed subject of 'statuere'. 'pro Palladio, pro numine laeso' — 'in exchange for the Palladium, for the divinity wronged'; 'laeso' is a participle, 'injured'. 'statuere' = 'statuerunt'. 'nefas quae triste piaret' — 'quae' is a relative with the subjunctive of purpose, 'to atone for'. 'nefas' is a violation of divine law (the opposite of 'fas', line 157).

sentences.t:
Hanc tamen immensam Calchas attollere molem
roboribus textis caeloque educere iussit,
ne recipi portis, aut duci in moenia possit,
neu populum antiqua sub religione tueri.
sentences.l:
This, however, immense, Calchas to raise, the mass,
with woven oak, and up to the sky to lift ordered,
so that it not be received by gates or be led into the walls,
nor the people under ancient religion protect.
sentences.i: Yet this immense bulk Calchas ordered them to raise high, built of interwoven oak, and carry up into the sky, so that it could not be taken in by the gates or drawn within the walls, nor protect the people under the old faith.
sentences.n: 'Hanc tamen' — 'tamen' means 'yet', that is, even so (in spite of its being an offering). 'immensam… molem' — 'molem' is the object of 'attollere' and 'educere', infinitives after 'iussit'. 'roboribus textis' — 'robur' is oak, 'woven oak' and 'textis' echoes 'intexunt' at line 16 (there the timber is fir). 'caelo… educere' — 'to lead up to the sky', in the dative of direction. 'ne… possit' is a negative purpose clause. 'neu' = 'ne… ve', 'nor', continuing the purpose clause with 'tueri' (the subject 'it'). 'antiqua sub religione' — the old cult of Pallas: the horse, if brought in, would shield Troy as the Palladium once did.

sentences.i: For if your hand should desecrate Minerva's gift, then great ruin (may the gods turn that omen on Calchas himself!) would fall on Priam's realm and the Phrygians;
sentences.n: The reason for the great size, given as Calchas's warning. 'Nam' states the cause. 'vestra manus' — 'your hand', Sinon here speaks to the Trojans. 'violasset' = 'violavisset', pluperfect subjunctive (a contraction). 'dona Minervae' — Minerva is the Roman name of Athena. 'tum… futurum' — the apodosis of the condition in indirect speech: 'futurum (esse)' is the future infinitive, 'would come'. The bracket is a parenthetic wish: 'quod… omen… convertant' is a subjunctive of wish, 'may the gods turn that omen!' (an apotropaic wish to avert it), 'in ipsum' — most naturally 'on Calchas himself', who prophesies it; 'prius' is 'rather, first'. 'Phrygibus' — the Phrygians, the Trojans. 'imperio' is a dative: 'destruction for Priam's rule'.

sentences.t:
sin manibus vestris vestram ascendisset in urbem,
ultro Asiam magno Pelopea ad moenia bello
venturam, et nostros ea fata manere nepotes.”
sentences.l:
but if by your hands into your city it had climbed,
of its own accord Asia to Pelops's walls with a great war
would come, and our descendants those fates await.”
sentences.i: but if by your own hands it climbed into your city, then Asia would of her own accord march in great war upon the walls of Pelops, and that those fates await our descendants.”
sentences.n: 'sin' = 'but if' (the opposite condition), with 'ascendisset' (pluperfect subjunctive), 'manibus vestris', 'vestram… urbem' ('your city'). 'ultro' means 'of her own accord' (it is Asia that takes the offensive). 'Asiam… venturam' and 'ea fata manere' are the infinitive clauses of the same indirect speech, the first with 'esse' left out. 'Pelopea ad moenia' — 'Pelopea' is the adjective from Pelops (father of Atreus), so 'Pelops's walls' are Mycenae and, by extension, Greece. 'nostros… nepotes' — the Trojans' descendants: Sinon now says 'ours' of the Trojans, so enrolling himself among them, a final touch of flattery. The reversal is the trap: the horse's entry is made to promise a Trojan victory. The closing mark is Greenough's: Sinon's second speech ends here.
